sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: The service supports event discovery and ticket purchases. Many customers can compete for the same seat.
Browsing shows an availability estimate. The booking path decides which customer can purchase each ticket.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: Users can view event details, venue layouts, and ticket availability.
Users can search events by text, location, date, and other supported filters.
Users can reserve seats temporarily. They can purchase the seats after payment succeeds.
An abandoned reservation must expire so another customer can claim the seats.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: A seat must not have two successful purchases. Booking correctness takes priority when requests conflict.
Search should take less than 500 ms. The design must handle a popular event with 10 million interested users.
Reservations have short lifetimes. The system must recover from interrupted checkout, payment retries, and application failures.
Reads can exceed writes by approximately 100 to one. Cached availability does not authorize a purchase.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: Event, Performer, and Venue describe the performance, schedule, location, and seating layout.
Ticket identifies a seat at an event. It records the price and purchase state. The reservation design also tracks temporary ownership.
Booking groups one customer's tickets under a durable ID. It records the total price and payment state.
User identifies the authenticated buyer. An idempotency key distinguishes a retry from a new checkout attempt.

sections.title: API
points: GET /events/:eventId returns event details and the seat map. The search API accepts filters and pagination parameters.
A reservation request claims selected tickets temporarily. The response contains a booking ID and expiration time.
A confirmation request supplies the booking ID and payment token. A status endpoint can support recovery after a lost response.
Each state change checks current ownership and purchase state. A reservation created earlier may have expired or changed owners.

sections.title: 1) Browse and search
points: The Event Service reads event, venue, and performer records from the database. The initial Search Service also queries that database.
The deep dives add caches and Elasticsearch. Committed database changes must reach the search index.
Seat availability changes more often than event descriptions. It needs a shorter refresh period and authoritative booking checks.

flows.title: View an event in the initial design
steps: The client requests an event by ID through the API Gateway.
The API Gateway routes the request to the Event Service.
The Event Service reads the event, venue, performer, and ticket information from the database.
The service returns the data needed for the event page and seat map.

flows.title: Search the initial event database
steps: The client sends search terms and filters to the API Gateway.
The API Gateway forwards the request to the Search Service.
The Search Service queries the event database for matching records.
The service returns a page of results. The later search design replaces this path with Elasticsearch.

sections.title: 2) Book tickets
points: The initial Booking Service checks ticket availability and creates a booking within one PostgreSQL transaction.
The database must reject a competing claim. Row locks or optimistic concurrency checks protect the ticket update.
This initial design checks availability after the user enters payment details. The reservation deep dive improves that experience.
Payment callbacks can repeat. An idempotent handler must return or retain the existing booking result without another purchase.

flows.title: Claim tickets in the initial design
steps: The client submits selected ticket IDs to the Booking Service through the API Gateway.
The Booking Service starts a PostgreSQL transaction. It checks whether the selected tickets are available.
The transaction updates ticket state and inserts the booking record.
A conflicting claim makes the transaction fail. Otherwise, the committed booking result returns to the client.
The reservation deep dive adds a temporary hold before payment. The payment outcome must agree with the final committed booking.

sections.title: 1) Reservation expiry
points: A database transaction must not remain open while the customer completes checkout. Long locks block other work and occupy connections.
One alternative stores a reserved state and expiration in PostgreSQL. A short transaction can reclaim an expired reservation.
A cleanup job can remove expired state. Correctness must also check expiration during a new claim.
Diagram 6 uses Redis ticket locks with a ten-minute lifetime. PostgreSQL still prevents duplicate purchases if a lock expires or fails.
Final confirmation must check the current booking and ownership. A late payment for an invalid booking needs reconciliation or a refund.

flows.title: Reserve through Redis and confirm payment
steps: The customer selects tickets. The Booking Service attempts expiring Redis locks for those ticket IDs.
If any required lock fails, the service releases this attempt's acquired locks. It reports that the group is unavailable.
The service records an in-progress booking. It returns the booking ID and the ten-minute checkout deadline.
The client obtains a Stripe payment token. The Booking Service creates the payment attempt for that booking.
Stripe sends the payment result to the webhook handler. The handler checks the booking state and current ownership.
For a valid successful payment, a PostgreSQL transaction marks the tickets sold and the booking confirmed.
A repeated callback keeps the existing result. A paid but invalid reservation needs reconciliation or a refund.
The service releases its remaining locks after success. Abandoned locks expire automatically.

sections.title: 2) Scale event views
points: A load balancer distributes requests across stateless Event Service instances.
Redis or Memcached can store event metadata. Separate read capacity protects booking work from browsing spikes.
Cache expiration and invalidation limit stale results. The Event Service can show live reservations using entries with expiration timestamps.

sections.title: 3) Handle high-demand onsales
points: SSE can send seat changes to connected browsers. This reduces repeated polling but cannot guarantee that a displayed seat remains available.
A virtual waiting room admits customers at a rate that the Booking Service can support.
The source stores admitted sessions in Redis with an expiration. The Booking Service checks admission before it accepts reservations.
Queue position updates help waiting customers. A reconnect must preserve queue identity. Admission alone does not reserve a seat.

flows.title: Admit customers through the waiting room
steps: The client joins the virtual queue. The system records its queue identity and opens an SSE or WebSocket connection.
The queue selects customers from its front as booking capacity becomes available.
The system records the admitted session in Redis with an expiration. It notifies the client that checkout is available.
The Booking Service checks that admission record before it accepts a reservation request.
An admitted customer still follows the normal ticket-claim process. Queue admission does not guarantee a ticket.

sections.title: 4) Improve search
points: Database indexes and full-text search can support the first design. Elasticsearch supports more complex text queries and spelling variations.
Change data capture updates Elasticsearch from PostgreSQL. Search caches must include every relevant filter in their keys.
A search result can become stale before checkout. CDN caching is suitable only when the same query returns equivalent public results.

flows.title: Query the search index
steps: PostgreSQL commits an event change. Change data capture sends that change to Elasticsearch.
The Search Service receives search terms, filters, and pagination parameters.
It queries Elasticsearch for matching events. A suitable cache can answer repeated equivalent requests.
The service returns the result page. Ticket availability remains subject to the booking path's current checks.

sections.title: Final Design
points: The Event Service serves cached event details. The Search Service uses Elasticsearch and suitable query caches.
The Booking Service uses expiring Redis reservations and conditional PostgreSQL writes. Stripe callbacks update each booking idempotently.
The waiting room controls admission during popular events. Seat updates improve the display while the booking database protects ownership.
